extracted.intended_audience: scholars of public policy and political science; regulatory practitioners; congressional and agency staff interested in rulemaking and agenda-setting
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the ways administrative delegation affects what problems and solution heuristics receive sustained attention (agenda openness vs closure), the mechanisms that narrow administrative agendas, empirical indicators of such closure, and institutional remedies (participation programs, congressional capacity, sunsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda closure / agenda limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Agenda limitation may be desirable but may also worsen the quality of public problem solving... delegation to administrative agencies presumes, if it does not favor, agenda closure - a tightly constrained focus on a limited set of issues to which the legislature has entrusted the agency’s authority and resources, and a narrow set of methods and consiliaria (experts, lawyers, adversaries, commenters) from which the agency seeks and gets its information.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a primary evaluative dimension: assess whether an institution’s agenda is tightly constrained vs open; note tradeoffs (specialization/expertise versus narrowed consideration of alternatives). Examples: agencies' narrow focus on certain policy tools; anti-patterns include reliance on a small set of advisers and methods. Consider normative stance (agenda closure can be a feature or a bug).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjuncture requirement for policy change (problem streams and solution streams)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Policy change happens under the conjuncture of solution streams and policy streams (given a structure or moment of political opportunity)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether both a recognized problem stream and an available solution stream are present; absence of either reduces chance of change. Use Kingdon-style criteria: presence of a window of opportunity, alignment of problem and solution. Empirically, check timing and matching of problem framing with solution proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation/congruence of agendas (public vs legislative vs administrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is an impressive congruence between the priorities of the public and the priorities of Congress across time... while the problem agenda for Congress is wider than that of the public, this macro-correspondence points to a form of representative democracy..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which an actor’s agenda (agency or legislature) corresponds to public priorities. For agencies, measure divergence from congressional/public priorities as evidence of democratic slippage. Data sources: public opinion measures, congressional agenda studies, agency rulemaking topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic diversity (breadth of problem-solving heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The idea that problem-solving... concerns different sets of tools or approaches... teams of problem solvers are better off with a broader set of heuristics when considering complex problems" (Hong & Page et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heuristic diversity as a quality metric: broader disciplinary and methodological inputs → better problem solving. Evaluate presence/absence of diverse heuristics (legal, economic, public-health, implementation, administrative expertise). Anti-patterns: monocultural reliance on a single method or discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative case for agenda democracy / openness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The demos must have the exclusive opportunity to decide how matters are to be placed on the agenda of matters that are to be decided by means of the democratic process." (Dahl)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat democratic access to agenda-setting as a normative criterion: evaluate procedural openness (hearings, comments, petitions, petition-response systems) and the extent to which lay/public voices can shape agenda items. Weigh normative value against efficiency trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative specialization as a mechanism of closure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Administrative Structure. The very fundaments of administrative government entail topical specialization. It is a feature, and not a bug, of administrative government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether topical specialization produces systematically narrower toolkits and solution sets. Consider moderating factors (interagency working groups, presidential management). Score: degree of siloing across policy domains; evidence of missing cross-domain heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying dynamics and concentration of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Public comments and non-comment meetings with rulemaking agencies come disproportionately from the regulated industry... and within that, a small set of players... especially bank-holding companies (BHCs)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by measuring concentration of meetings/comments, share of submissions from regulated entities vs public interest groups, and diversity of stakeholder types. Anti-pattern: domination by a few firms or trade associations. Use notice-and-comment data, meeting logs, and lobby disclosure records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural capture
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cultural capture: regulators have to spend an inordinate amount of time talking to the entities they regulate... status dynamics and continual proximity may mean... convergence of views of ways of approaching problems." (Kwak)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose cultural capture by assessing convergence of regulator and regulated-industry framings, routine personnel exchange, and patterns of empathy/deference in meeting transcripts. Look for soft mechanisms beyond revolving-door contracts: shared language, interpretive frames, and social proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/proximity effects on representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The physical proximity of many administrators to certain constituents (and not others) may exacerbate this dynamic... those who must travel further to (or who do not have delegates employed in) the capital city are less likely to be represented there."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure geographic/accessibility biases in participation (who attends in-person meetings, who has lobby presence in capital). Consider telepresence/remote engagement as mitigations. Use travel/time constraints as an explanatory variable for underrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators of heuristic agenda closure (case signals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples cited as potential evidence: FDA less receptive to patient voices historically; agencies' narrow conception of 'science' in COVID; financial regulators' receptivity to 'financial innovation' pre-2007; dominance of large firms in Dodd-Frank rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these case patterns as empirical indicators. When evaluating a rulemaking or agency behavior: look for signs such as narrow conceptions of evidence/science, sectoral bias in commenters/meetings, failure to consider alternative heuristics, and temporal patterns of attention shifting away from certain publics. Use case comparison rather than single-instance inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation mechanisms to open administrative spaces (advisory committees, consumer participation, proxy advocates)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The function of advisory committees... may be less to draw on expertise per se than to open up the process to a wider set of public inputs... systematic embedment of consumer... voices (e.g., California’s Public Participation Program; NAIC’s Consumer Participation Program)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these institutional designs by their ability to diversify inputs: composition of advisory bodies, representativeness of consumer reps, coordination among proxy advocates, and evidence of substantive influence (Schwarcz MLR example). Note mixed evidence; check for astroturfing or industry-influenced 'consumer' voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intergovernmental/proxy participation as mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: "In federal rulemaking... participation of state governments... is associated with less industry influence in federal rulemaking outcomes (Yackee 2014)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sovereign or intermediary actors (states, local governments, professional bodies) as proxies for broader publics. Evaluate whether their participation reduces industry dominance and introduces different heuristics. Measure cross-jurisdictional engagement levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthening congressional capacity and sunsets as remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: "Strengthening institutions that serve all members (CBO, GAO) and domain-specific committees... consider 'sunsets' for agency regulations or even legislative delegations... compelling the legislature to revisit these problems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as institutional design criteria: assess feasibility and expected benefits of increasing legislative analytic capacity and periodic legislative reauthorization (sunsets). Consider cost, political feasibility, and whether such changes complement (not substitute for) administrative reforms. Cite historical examples (Colorado 1976; FACA advisory committee sunsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation trade-off: expertise vs fidelity and venue openness vs restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: "Delegation trades off not only expertise against the administrators’ preferences... but a plausibly more open venue with that of a more restricted agenda."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating delegation arrangements, explicitly weigh (a) gains in expertise/technical capacity against (b) losses in representativeness and agenda breadth. Use this trade-off to guide design choices: degree of statutory detail, oversight intensity, required procedural openness, and scope of delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of 'agenda' (multiple definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Author’s enumerated understandings: 1) menu from which final choice is made (1a/1b), 2) most important problem, 3) shortlist of the possible, 4) common sense, 5) set of things that are public, 6) set of things that are political, 7) heuristics available to interpret problems, 8) the persons giving voice to agenda items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require analysts to specify which conception of 'agenda' they are using when evaluating openness/closure. Different measures and remedies follow from each definition (e.g., measuring publicness vs measuring heuristic sets vs measuring speaker composition). Use the list to clarify operationalization in empirical work.
